summary: Client-side retry + small connection pool causing serialized requests and perceived inference slowdowns
description:
Issue summary:
Customer (Narrative Labs) reports a regression in observed inference latency starting 2026-03-11. SDK metrics show long tail per-request latency despite backend token-generation latency remaining stable.

Impact:
High: user-facing features that stream completions show multi-second stalls before any tokens are emitted; throughput appears limited under concurrent load. Several 3rd-party alerts triggered for elevated P99 latency.

Environment:
- Customer using Redwood Go SDK v0.9.3 against hosted API in us-east, Dedicated plan.
- Default SDK HTTP client settings were used: max_connections=10, max_idle_conns_per_host=2, max_retries=5, backoff_strategy=linear(200ms).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Run load test: 200 concurrent chat requests that stream token-by-token (avg prompt length 180 tokens).
2) Observe overall client-side request queueing and long waits before connection established/stream init.
3) Reduce client concurrency to 20 and latency tails disappear.

Observed behavior:
- Backend traces (serving runtime) show nominal generation time (~30-80ms/token).
- Client-side observed TTFB (time to first byte) often 800ms-2.5s under concurrency.
- SDK logs show many retries and repeated connection lease waits.
- No sustained 5xx from API; occasional 429s during bursts.

Logs & snippets (customer attached):
- SDK http pool warnings: "connection pool exhausted, waiting for free connection"
- Retry logs: "attempt=3 status=429 wait=0.2s" repeated across requests
- tcpdump shows many SYN/FIN churn when connections closed prematurely by client due to retry logic

Initial hypothesis:
- The customer SDK config (small pool + high retry count + short linear backoff) serializes concurrent requests onto too few connections. Retries happen synchronously and block other requests waiting for free sockets, producing an illusion of a slow backend.
- Also possible interaction with streaming (chunked transfer) keeping connections occupied longer, reducing effective concurrency.

Investigation notes:
- Correlated SDK pool exhaustion events with periods of high retries and temporary 429 rate-limits.
- Traced a sample request path: request A hits transient 429 -> SDK retries immediately on same thread -> consumes pool slot for duration of retry/backoff -> request B waits for free connection -> perceived latency increases.
- Experimented in staging by increasing max_connections to 50 and reducing max_retries to 2 with exponential backoff + jitter. Observed P95/P99 client latency drop by ~60%-75% under same load.
- Confirmed streaming requests keep sockets open for duration of token streaming; long-lived streams reduce pool throughput if pool size is small.

Workarounds recommended to customer (applied and validated):
- Increase SDK connection pool sizes: max_connections=50, max_idle_conns_per_host=20.
- Reduce max_retries to 1-2 for interactive/streaming flows.
- Switch backoff to exponential with jitter (base=100ms, max=1s) to avoid synchronized retry storms.
- Enable HTTP/2 multiplexing in the SDK (if supported) to allow multiple streams over single connection and reduce connection churn.
- Use client-side circuit-breaker to fail fast on sustained 429s and fallback to degraded UX rather than queue.

Resolution summary:
- Customer applied recommended SDK changes and observed immediate improvement. Support confirmed backend serving metrics unchanged, pointing to client-side configuration as root cause.
- Support created SDK change request to update Go SDK defaults for streaming/high-concurrency clients and to add a QA guide in Confluence.

Follow-ups / Action items:
- PR to SDK: set safer defaults for streaming workloads and expose clear docs (github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-go/pull/812).
- KB article: patterns for streaming + retries + pools (confluence.internal.redwood/KB/connection-pools-and-retries).
- Monitor assigned to ENG on-call for 72 hours to ensure no recurrence.

resolution: Root cause: client-side SDK misconfiguration (small connection pool + high retry count + linear backoff) combined with streaming requests occupied connections for extended periods. This caused connection pool exhaustion and serialized retries, producing perceived slowdowns. Resolution: customer updated SDK settings (increased pool, reduced retries, switched to exponential backoff with jitter, enabled HTTP/2 when possible). SDK defaults and docs updated to prevent recurrence.
